ch6_ex1_q1: Think of a trapezium as a rectangle whose width is the average of the parallel sides: $\frac{7.3+15.2}{2} = 11.25$, so the area is $11.25 \times 6.1$.
Quick estimate: about $11 \times 6 = 66$, so an answer near $68.6\text{ mm}^2$ is sensible.
ch6_ex1_q2: An ellipse is a circle stretched in one direction, so $\pi r^2 = \pi r \times r$ becomes $\pi a b$. If $a = b$ you get the circle formula back.
Check: the ellipse must be smaller than the $16 \times 10$ bounding rectangle ($160\text{ cm}^2$) and bigger than a circle of radius 5 ($\approx 78.5\text{ cm}^2$).
ch6_ex1_q3: Option A ($9.6$) is $3.2 \times 2 \times 1.5$, which is the volume in $\text{m}^3$, not a surface area. Watch for distractors built from the wrong formula.
Sketch the net: three different rectangles, each appearing twice (top/bottom, front/back, left/right).
ch6_ex1_q4: Since $r = \frac{d}{2}$, $4\pi r^2 = \pi d^2$. So you can go straight to $\pi \times 15^2 = 225\pi$ without halving.
Memory aid: a sphere's surface is exactly 4 times the area of its 'equator' circle, $\pi r^2$.
ch6_ex1_q5: Any pointed solid (cone or pyramid) has $V = \frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}$. When the base area is given, you don't need $\pi$ or $r$ at all.
Units check: $\text{cm}^2 \times \text{cm} = \text{cm}^3$, so the answer is a volume.
ch6_ex1_q6: Find the whole ring first: $\pi(5^2 - 2^2) = 21\pi$. Removing a $45^\circ$ sector leaves $\frac{315}{360} = \frac{7}{8}$ of it, so the area is $\frac{7}{8} \times 21\pi$.
Use $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$, not $\pi(R - r)^2$: squaring the 3 cm width gives the wrong answer.
ch6_ex1_q7: Alternative method: take the full $240 \times 130$ rectangle and subtract the missing $80 \times 30$ corner: $31\,200 - 2400 = 28\,800\text{ m}^2$. Both methods should agree.
Dividing by 1000 just moves the decimal point 3 places, so $28\,800\text{ m}^2$ is 28.8 lots of $\$30$.
ch6_ex1_q8: $l = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{87.25} \approx 9.34$. The slant height must always be longer than the vertical height, so if your $l$ is less than 9, recheck.
Don't include the circular base: it is hidden where the hemisphere and cone join.
ch6_ex1_q9: Spot the 3-4-5 Pythagorean triple: with a 3 and a hypotenuse of 5, the missing side is 4 without any calculation.
Only the two perpendicular sides go into $\frac{1}{2}bh$: $\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6$, never the hypotenuse.
ch6_ex1_q10: Shortcut: a cone of height 15 holds the same as a cylinder of height $\frac{15}{3} = 5$ with the same base. So the total is like one cylinder of height $25$: $\pi \times 5^2 \times 25 \approx 1963.5$.
Option D ($7854$) is exactly 4 times the correct answer: that is what happens if the diameter 10 is used as the radius. A factor-of-4 error usually means radius and diameter were mixed up.
ch6_ex1_q11: Test the options with special cases: if $y = x$ the solid is a prism, so $V = hx^2$; if $y = 0$ it is a pyramid, so $V = \frac{1}{3}hx^2$. Only D passes both.
Dimension check: a volume needs length$^3$. Option A and B have no $h$, so they are only length$^2$ and cannot be volumes.
ch6_ex1_q12: Estimate first: $\frac{4}{3}\pi \approx 4.19$, so $r^3 \approx 384.66 \div 4.19 \approx 92$. Since $4.5^3 \approx 91$, $r \approx 4.5$ is believable.
On a calculator use the $\sqrt[3]{\ }$ key, or raise to the power $(1/3)$ with brackets: $(\ldots)^{(1/3)}$.
ch6_ex1_q13: Use scale factors: the volume changes by (radius factor)$^2 \times$ (height factor) $= 2^2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 2$.
Test with easy numbers: $r = 1, h = 2$ gives $\frac{2}{3}\pi$; $r = 2, h = 1$ gives $\frac{4}{3}\pi$, which is double.
ch6_ex1_q14: Here $s = 10$, so the product is $10 \times 1 \times 6 \times 3 = 180$ and $A = \sqrt{180} = 6\sqrt{5} \approx 13.4$.
Check: each of $s-a$, $s-b$, $s-c$ must be positive. A zero or negative value means the three sides cannot form a triangle.
ch6_ex1_q15: A half-full can holds the same as a full can of half the height, so you can use $h = 7.15$ directly: $\pi \times 3.2^2 \times 7.15 \approx 230$.
Estimate: $\pi r^2 \approx 3 \times 10 = 30$, times $7$ is about $210$, so 230 mL is reasonable.
